title: Serving open models
summary: Running open-weight models yourself with a serving engine (vLLM, SGLang), a local runtime (Ollama, Foundry Local) or Kubernetes (KAITO on AKS), and knowing when a managed deployment is the better answer.
useIf: You need custom or open weights, steady high volume, offline use, or control that managed deployments cannot give.
avoidIf: Residency is the only driver and a data zone or regional deployment meets it, or you lack GPU operations skill and steady load.

explain.md: A **serving engine** turns weights into an HTTP endpoint and keeps GPUs busy. **vLLM** (UC Berkeley origin) uses PagedAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, speculative decoding and many quantization formats. The 2023 paper reports 2 to 4x throughput at the same latency against prior systems [[r16]] [[r17]]. **SGLang** adds RadixAttention for KV reuse across requests with shared prefixes and compressed finite state machines for structured output, with up to 6.4x throughput reported [[r18]]. Both are vendor or author-reported numbers on their own benchmarks.

explain.title: Is self-hosting cheaper?
explain.expr: cost per million tokens = GPU cost per hour / (million tokens per hour at full load x utilization)

vars.v: share of the hour the GPU does useful work

explain.example: Illustrative numbers: a GPU at $6 per hour that can serve 3 million tokens per hour at full load costs $2 per million tokens at 100% utilization and $4 per million at 50%. Idle GPUs make self-hosting expensive.

explain.md: Microsoft advises starting with Global Standard unless residency, reserved throughput or batch forces a change [[r24]]. Strict residency usually starts with Data Zone or Regional deployments before self-hosting. Pick the engine by workload: vLLM is a general-purpose engine, SGLang suits shared-prefix and structured-output work, and a local runtime suits one user on one device. Whatever you pick, you also take on safety layers, patching and capacity planning that a managed service handles.

whereToUse: Serving fine-tuned or open-weight models that a managed catalog does not host
High, steady request volume where GPU utilization stays high
Offline or edge apps that must run on a laptop or device
Structured-output or shared-prefix workloads that benefit from SGLang or vLLM prefix reuse
Kubernetes shops that want a managed add-on to deploy open models on AKS

use: You need weights, tuning or network control a managed API cannot provide
Load is steady enough to keep GPUs busy
You have staff for GPU capacity, upgrades and monitoring
avoid: Bursty or low volume that leaves GPUs idle
Residency is the only requirement and a Data Zone or Regional deployment satisfies it
You expect Foundry Local to act as a multi-user server

Offline or single-user need appears: on-device runtime beats a central server

pitfalls.symptom: GPU bill is high and latency is still poor
pitfalls.cause: Low utilization and no batching or prefix reuse
pitfalls.fix: Measure utilization, enable continuous batching and prefix caching and re-run the cost formula against managed pricing.

pitfalls.cause: GPU SKU below compute capability 8.0, or an unsupported region or node pool type
pitfalls.fix: Check the prerequisites: NVIDIA compute capability 8.0 or later, Azure CLI 2.76.0 or later, Linux node pools, public Azure region.

pitfalls.symptom: Prototype on Foundry Local falls over with many users
pitfalls.cause: It is an on-device runtime, not a multi-user server
pitfalls.fix: Move to vLLM or Triton Inference Server for shared serving.

scenarios.title: Residency with no GPU team
scenarios.situation: A team must keep inference inside the EU. Volume is moderate and spiky. No one on the team runs GPUs.
constraints: Inference must stay in the EU data zone
unknowns: Does the needed model exist as a Data Zone deployment?
scenarios.question: Where does the model run?

options.name: Foundry Local on a server
options.why: It is an on-device runtime and Microsoft points to vLLM or Triton for multi-user serving.
options.tradeoff: Right for an offline single-user app.

options.name: Managed Data Zone or Regional deployment
options.why: Meets residency without GPUs and handles spikes through capacity you rent.
options.tradeoff: You get the catalog's models and its quota limits.

options.name: Self-host vLLM on AKS with KAITO
options.why: Full control and inference in a region you pick.
options.tradeoff: GPU cost when idle, ops work and your own safety layers.

flips.if: The model you need is not offered in a Data Zone deployment
flips.then: Self-hosting becomes the way to keep it in region.
Re-run the cost formula, since GPUs may beat per-token pricing.

scenarios.takeaway: Residency usually starts with managed zones, not GPUs.

scenarios.title: Field app with no connectivity
scenarios.situation: Technicians use a tablet app in places with no network. Each device serves one user. Data must not leave the device.
unknowns: How large can the model be?
scenarios.question: How do you serve the model?

options.name: Call a managed API
options.why: It needs connectivity and sends data off the device.
options.tradeoff: Right when users are online and policy allows cloud processing.

options.name: Embed an on-device runtime such as Foundry Local
options.why: It runs on ONNX Runtime, needs no Azure subscription and adds about 20 MB to the app.
options.tradeoff: Model size and speed are bounded by device hardware.

options.name: Central vLLM cluster with sync on reconnect
options.tradeoff: Does not work offline and adds sync complexity.

flips.if: Devices have a reliable link and policy allows cloud
flips.then: A managed deployment is simpler and stronger.

flips.if: Hardware is too weak for the model
flips.then: Use a smaller or quantized model or a hybrid with deferred cloud calls.

scenarios.takeaway: Offline and per-device privacy point to on-device runtimes.

scenarios.title: High steady volume with tuned weights
scenarios.situation: A platform team serves a fine-tuned open model to many internal apps. Traffic is steady around the clock. The team already runs Kubernetes and has H100-class and T4 GPU pools.
unknowns: What utilization do you expect per GPU?
Which pools meet the compute capability rule?
scenarios.question: How do you host it?

options.name: vLLM through KAITO on AKS using GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or later
options.why: Custom weights need self-hosting, steady load keeps utilization high and KAITO integrates vLLM.
options.tradeoff: You run capacity, upgrades and safety layers, and the add-on lags upstream by one release.

options.name: KAITO on the T4 pool
options.why: KAITO needs NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or later, so T4 and V100 are out.
options.tradeoff: T4 pools can still serve small workloads with other tooling.

options.name: Managed catalog model only
options.tradeoff: Your fine-tuned weights cannot run there, so you lose the tuning.

flips.then: Re-evaluate managed pricing with the cost formula.

flips.if: Upstream vLLM features are needed sooner
flips.then: Run vLLM directly instead of the add-on.

scenarios.takeaway: Custom weights plus steady load justify GPUs. Check the hardware rules first.

quiz.q: Which is the right tool for multi-user serving according to Microsoft's Foundry Local docs?
options: Foundry Local itself, running on the server
A browser extension that proxies requests
quiz.explain: Foundry Local is an on-device runtime and Microsoft points to vLLM or Triton for multi-user serving. Ollama on a laptop is also a local tool.

quiz.q: A GPU costs $6 per hour and can serve 3 million tokens per hour at full load. At 50% utilization, what is the cost per million tokens?
quiz.hint: Effective throughput is full throughput times utilization.
quiz.explain: Effective throughput is 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 million tokens per hour. Cost is $6 / 1.5 = $4 per million tokens.

quiz.q: A KAITO workspace will not run. Which prerequisites should you check?
options: NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 8.0 or later
quiz.explain: KAITO needs compute capability 8.0 or later and Azure CLI 2.76.0 or later. It does not support Windows node pools, and T4 and V100 are below the capability rule.

flashcards.front: What does PagedAttention do in vLLM?
flashcards.back: It stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks to cut memory waste and allow more concurrent requests. The paper reports 2 to 4x throughput at the same latency.
SGLang's KV cache reuse across requests that share a prefix, using a radix tree. SGLang also uses compressed finite state machines for structured output.

flashcards.front: What GPU rule does KAITO on AKS impose?
flashcards.back: NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or later, so no T4 or V100. It also needs Azure CLI 2.76.0 or later and public Azure regions.
